P6g2: What impressed me the most was how they do authority. It's mandar obedeciendo, to lead by obeying: the representatives carry the decisions people made in the assemblies, and they have to answer to the people who gave them the mandate.
P12d2: One thing the Zapatistas themselves have been clear about is that people shouldn't import or export Zapatismo as a ready-made model. The useful thing isn't their diagram. It's how they learn: they build things and ask questions, and when they find out where the practice isn't working, they change the structure.
P15f2: One way an escuelita could fail is if it becomes a business, where residents spend their lives performing community for paying outsiders, and success gets measured by how many people come instead of how many daughter communities get started. A week of feeling transformed isn't what it's for. It's for teaching enough of the social and material system that some people can build it somewhere else.
P16b4: In my research, I also tried to follow what happened after the Escuelita. I found alumni networks, people bringing practices home, and organizing later on. What I didn't find was a clear chain from an Escuelita student to a newly founded communal institution, and then evidence of how its members and their kids actually did over time. Zapatista influence was already traveling internationally before the Escuelita, so a resemblance later on doesn't prove by itself that it came from the Escuelita. I'm borrowing a way of teaching and the ambition to replicate, and I'm not claiming the Zapatistas have already proved my whole model.
H0pub: The Best Model I’ve Seen: Zapatistas
CAP1pub: A Zapatista Schoolhouse. It reads: Worthy Rage (Digna Rabia)
P4pub: Oventik itself felt like a real dream. We played basketball with Zapatista youth on an outdoor court. People gave us talks about their history and philosophy, and I translated for my friends because my Spanish was better. Visitors from around the world were coming to learn and to make the communities less easy to attack in silence.
P5pub: The Zapatistas felt deeply spiritual to me. I also suspect there may be a private relationship with ayahuasca, but nobody told me that, and I present it only as my impression—not as fact.
P8pub: The Fire and the Word describes the movement growing from family to village, village to region, and region to larger structures. It also gives one of the most useful Zapatista principles for community design: build the practice first and develop the theory afterward. The autonomous municipalities came first; an association of them became a rehearsal for the Good Government Boards. When different municipalities encountered different problems and uneven progress, that experience generated another structure rather than being forced to fit the original plan.
CAP2pub: Escuelita Zapatista — The Zapatista school to teach outsiders their way of life
P1v2: In 2005, a few college buddies and I went down to Oventik, one of the Zapatista caracoles in Chiapas. We almost died several times getting there. The mountain road ran along cliffs, and our rental car was on its last legs, which is a great combination when you're on your way to visit a revolution.
P2v2: In San Cristóbal de las Casas, the only white man we met sat us down in a café and grilled us so directly that he seemed like a CIA agent. Why were we there? Who were we working with? What were our plans? When were we leaving?
P3v2: It made us feel important for a minute. We were just college kids in a dying rental car, but apparently the empire had questions for us. 😂
